It might be possible to encode something like Formulog in Datafun; however, although it has recently been shown that Datafun can be evaluated using semi-naive evaluation (Arntzenius and Krishnaswami, 2020), it is not clear to what extent other Datalog optimizations can be applied to Datafun programs. By combining Datalog with functional programming, Formulog, Flix, and Datafun are related to functional logic programming (Antoy and Hanus, 2010). The functional fragment of Formulog is less expressive than what is typically found in such languages, as Formulog functions are not first-class values and not higher-order.

Logic programming with constraints and formulas

The two dominant prior paradigms for combining logic programming and constraint solving are constraint logic programming (CLP) (Jaffar and Lassez, 1987; Jaffar and Maher, 1994) and constrained Horn clause (CHC) solving (Grebenshchikov et al., 2012; Gurfinkel et al., 2015; Hoder and Bjørner, 2012; Bjørner et al., 2015). As discussed in Section 6, these systems typically encode constraints as predicates, not terms, and thus support programming with constraints as things to be satisfied, rather than programming with formulas, which can be manipulated in more interesting ways (e.g., validity checking). In the context of static analysis, these systems have been used primarily for model checking, where a model of the input system is encoded using Horn clauses (Bjørner et al., 2015; Delzanno and Podelski, 1999; Flanagan, 2004; Fribourg and Richardson, 1996; Grebenshchikov et al., 2012). The rules depend on the program being analyzed, and the solutions to these rules reveal properties of the model; e.g., SeaHorn (Gurfinkel et al., 2015) checks programs by solving a CHC representation of their verification conditions. This differs than the approach taken in this paper, where the rules encode an analysis independent of the input program. The Datalog mode of μ\muZ (Hoder et al., 2011) can be thought of as a bottom-up CLP system with special support for abstract interpretation.

A few existing logic programming systems support programming with formulas (vs constraints); we would argue that none do so with the same richness and flexibility as Formulog. Codish et al. (2008) extend Prolog with an interface to a SAT solver. SICStus Prolog (Carlsson and Mildner, 2012), with its CLP extensions, has been used to write model checkers (Delzanno and Podelski, 1999; Fribourg and Richardson, 1996; Podelski and Rybalchenko, 2007; Grebenshchikov et al., 2012); these implementations typically rely on Prolog’s non-logical features, like assert, making it harder to apply high-level optimizations like parallelization. Calypso (Hackett, 2010; Aiken et al., 2007) is a Datalog variant that interfaces with external constraint solvers and has specialized support for bottom-up analyses. Calypso has been used with SAT and integer constraint solvers; in theory, it could be connected to an SMT solver. However, Formulog offers several advantages over Calypso for SMT-based analyses. First, Formulog’s approach to constructing formulas (via complex terms) and manipulating them (via its ML fragment) scales to the complex and heterogeneous formulas that arise in the SMT context, whereas Calypso’s approach to formulas (opaque terms, constructed via predicates) would be cumbersome in this setting. Second, Formulog’s type system supports the construction of expressive (and safe) formulas involving user-defined terms such as algebraic data types and uninterpreted functions. Third, the ML fragment of Formulog goes a long way towards making it practical for SMT-based analyses, by closing the gap between specification and implementation, and improving ergonomics and performance.

The logic programming language λ\lambdaProlog provides a natural way to represent logical formulas using a form of higher-order abstract syntax based on λ\lambda-terms and higher-order unification (Pfenning and Elliott, 1988; Miller and Nadathur, 1987). Although this representation simplifies some aspects of using formulas, moving to a higher-order setting would complicate Formulog, widen the gap between Formulog and other Datalog variants, and potentially be an impediment to building a performant and scalable Formulog implementation. Answer set programming (ASP) uses specialized solvers to find a stable model (if it exists) of a set of Horn clauses (Gelfond and Lifschitz, 1988; Brewka et al., 2011). Common extensions support constraints on the shape of the stable model that will be found. ASP enables concise encoding of classic NP-complete constraint problems such as graph kk-coloring, but it is not as obviously applicable to static analysis problems.

Type system engineering

PLT Redex (Felleisen et al., 2009) and Spoofax (Kats and Visser, 2010) support exploratory type system engineering. PLT Redex supports a notion of judgment modeled explicitly on inference rules. Spoofax’s type engineering framework, Statix, uses a logic programming syntax to specify type systems, with a custom solver for resolving the binding information in scope graphs simultaneously with solving typing constraints (van Antwerpen et al., 2018). Both of these systems use custom approaches to finding typing derivations; neither supports SMT queries, but Statix’s custom solver can resolve constraint systems that might not always terminate in Formulog.

Solver-aided languages

ScalaZ3{{}^{\text{Z3}}} (Köksal et al., 2011) supports mixed computations combining normal Scala evaluation and Z3 solving; we avoid this level of integration. Smten (Uhler and Dave, 2013) is a solver-aided language that supports both concrete and symbolic evaluation; Rosette (Torlak and Bodik, 2013) is a framework for creating solver-aided languages that have this property.

8. Conclusion

Formulog is a domain-specific language for writing SMT-based static analyses that judiciously combines Datalog, ML, and SMT solving (via an external SMT solver). As demonstrated by our case studies, it makes it possible to concisely implement a range of SMT-based analyses — refinement type checking, bottom-up points-to analysis, and symbolic evaluation — in a way close to their formal specifications, while also making it possible to automatically and advantageously apply high-level optimizations to these analyses like parallelization and goal-directed rewriting.

Appendix A Formulog’s formal model

We define a ‘middleweight’ formal model of Formulog, designing a type system (Section B) and an operational semantics (Section C), relating the two in a proof of type safety (Section D).

Our model characterizes Formulog as a two-level system (Figure 15), comprising Datalog-esque Horn clauses HH and first-order functions FF; Horn clause “rules” are made up of premises PP, where each premise is a series of (possibly negated) atoms AA. Each atom AA either references a Datalog predicate or binds a variable to an expression ee. Expressions themselves have two mutually recursive modes: ordinary functional computation ee and quoted SMT terms `​ϕ​`\textsf{\`{}}{\phi}\textsf{\`{}}, which can include unquoted expressions ,​e\textbf{,}{e}.

The Datalog fragment of Formulog is fairly standard syntactically, up to the addition of the atomic form X=eX=e. We constrain premises to a sort of administrative normal form: predicate references apply only to variables, written p⁡(Xi→)p(\vec{X_{i}}), and expression constraints bind variables, as in Y=eY=e. Our implementation can handle compound premises like p⁡(e1,e2)p(e_{1},e_{2}); our formal model would require rewriting such a premise to three premises: p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y), X=e1X=e_{1}, and Y=e2Y=e_{2} (for some fresh XX and YY).

The functional programming fragment fully annotates the types on its functions FF; variable names in both fragments are written in capital letters. (Our implementation merely demands that the first letter be capitalized.) SMT variables are written using lowercase letters and annotated with their type, as in c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,t]​()c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,t](). As described in Section 3.3, our implementation allows any value to be used as the name of an SMT variable; here, without loss of generality, we treat SMT variables as being drawn from a distinct universe. Code in the functional fragment can treat Datalog relations as predicates, i.e., p⁡(vi→)p(\vec{v_{i}}) returns true\mathrm{true} when vi→∈p\vec{v_{i}}\in p. In our implementation, some elements of vi→\vec{v_{i}} can be the wildcard ??, turning a Datalog predicate into a list. For example, if p⊆𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅×𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]p\subseteq\mathsf{bool}\times\mathsf{bv[32]}, then: p⁡(true,42)p(\mathrm{true},42) yields a 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool}; p⁡(??,42)p(\texttt{??},42) returns a list of 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool}s bb such that p⁡(b,42)p(b,42) holds; p⁡(true,??)p(\mathrm{true},\texttt{??}) returns a list of 𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]\mathsf{bv[32]}s nn such that p⁡(true,n)p(\mathrm{true},n) holds; p⁡(??,??)p(\texttt{??},\texttt{??}) returns a list of 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅×𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]\mathsf{bool}\times\mathsf{bv[32]}, i.e., the relation pp. We don’t include this behavior in our formal model.

The set of available base types BB must include 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool} at a minimum; any other SMT-embeddable base types are acceptable, e.g., kk-width bit vectors for a statically known kk.

As a matter of notation, we write ei→\vec{e_{i}} for a metavariable ee to mean a possibly empty sequence of ees, indexed by ii. When more than one variable shares the same index, we mean that those sequences must be of the same length (e.g., in the 𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁\mathsf{match} syntax, each branch of a match is a triple of a constructor cc, a vector of variable names for cc’s arguments, and a corresponding single expression).

Appendix B Formulog’s type system

We begin by presenting type checking rules for Formulog (Figures 16,  17,  18, and 19). Our implementation of Formulog not only performs type checking, but can also perform type inference, e.g., automatically finding type variable substitutions.

Our types are broken into two levels: types τ\tau and pre-types tt. Every pre-type tt can be directly considered as a type, but there are two additional types: t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt}, the type of SMT formulas yielding tt, and t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym}, the type of SMT variables of type tt. We factor the syntax in this way to prevent anomalies like 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅​𝗌𝗆𝗍​𝗌𝗆𝗍{{\mathsf{bool}}~\mathsf{smt}}~\mathsf{smt}, which would mean SMT formulas that yield SMT formulas that yield booleans. It is not the case, however, that every pre-type tt is necessarily representable as an SMT type, because data types may contain SMT formulas as arguments; we discuss how we categorize SMT-representable types shortly.

Before we begin, some further notational clarification. Rules are named by their primary subjects followed by a hyphen and a descriptive name. Whenever we use indices in rules, we will always map (stating a single premise in terms of the index, e.g., prog\mathrm{prog}-WF) or fold (stating first, indexed, and last, e.g., X→​τ→\vec{X}\vec{\tau}-All) over the sequence. We omit the indices when selecting an element of a sequence or set (as in, e.g., ee-Match in Figure 18).

All of our typing rules are in terms of a fixed set of data type declarations Δ\Delta and program declarations Φ\Phi (Figure 15). Data type declarations Δ\Delta map data type names DD to some number of type arguments αi→\vec{\alpha_{i}} and a set of constructors cj→\vec{c_{j}}, each of which takes some number of arguments of type τk→\vec{\tau_{k}}; each cjc_{j} can have a different number of arguments. Program declarations Φ\Phi collect the signatures of first-order polymorphic functions f:∀α→,τ→→τf:\forall\vec{\alpha},\vec{\tau}\rightarrow\tau, uninterpreted functions for use in the SMT solver 𝑢𝑓:t→→t\mathit{uf}:\vec{t}\rightarrow t, and relations p⊆τi→p\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}.

The highest level typing rule is prog\mathrm{prog}-WF (Figure 16), which ensures that the declarations are well formed and each part of the program is well formed.

The context and type well formedness rules (Figure 16) are mostly straightforward, type well formedness being the most interesting. Each type can be found to be well formed in either SMT mode 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}—i.e., it can be exported to the SMT solver–or in expression mode 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}, meaning it cannot be. There is a sub-moding relationship: well formed types at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt} are also well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}, but not necessarily vice-versa: for example, there is no way to export an SMT formula or variable as the object of another SMT formula, only as a constituent. We assume that all Formulog constants are SMT representable, i.e., ⋅⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍typeof(k)\cdot\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{typeof}(k) for all constants kk. Data type declarations are polymorphic, but we disallow phantom type variables. Data types can freely mutually recurse. Uninterpreted functions must be in terms of pre-types, and those pre-types must be closed and SMT representable (𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}); functions and relations can use any well formed types (𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}). Functions can be polymorphic but we disallow phantom type variables; relations have monomorphic types. Disallowing phantom types in constructors and functions and keeping relations monomorphic ensure that these forms are “reverse determinate”, i.e., the types of their arguments uniquely determine their types.

Since the declaration environments Δ\Delta and Φ\Phi are statically determined for an entire program, we typically leave them implicit. Implicit parameters are in gray in the boxed rule schemata in the figures. In proofs we will treat these parameters explicitly, but we conserve space by stating the rules without threading implicit parameters through. For example, the data type declarations Δ\Delta are necessary to ensure that tt-ADT only allows us to name data types that have actually been defined. Rather than threading Δ\Delta through every rule for context and type well formedness, we write Δ{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{\Delta}} in the rule schemata.

The type checking of the Datalog fragment of Formulog (Figure 17) must encode two Datalog invariants in addition to conventional typing constraints: the range restriction, i.e., every variable in the head of a rule appears somewhere in a premise; and appropriate binding, i.e., it is possible to interpret a Horn clause in such a way that all of the variables will be bound at the end. Our formal rules ensure that the program has correct binding structure for a left-to-right evaluation of each Horn clause. An implementation could determine whether or not an ordering would work and could reorder programs into an appropriate order automatically. Our formal model does not enforce that the dependencies between relations are appropriately stratified, though doing so would be easy: the relation-and-function call graph should not have any “negative” edge in a cycle, where a negative edge is created whenever there is a negated predicate in a rule body or a predicate is invoked as a function.

Concretely, HH-Clause ensures that (a) a left-to-right binding order produces some appropriate final context Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} (via the premise typing judgment), (b) the range restriction is satisfied, (Xi→⊆Γ′\vec{X_{i}}\subseteq\Gamma^{\prime}) by making sure that (c) every variable is well typed and bound (Γ′⊢Xi→,τi→⊳Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rhd\Gamma^{\prime}—having the same Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} means no new bindings were introduce when checking the head variables).

Premise typing Γ⊢P⊳Γ\Gamma\vdash P\rhd\Gamma and variable binding and typing Γ⊢x,τ⊳Γ\Gamma\vdash x,\tau\rhd\Gamma work together to generate appropriate types for each premise. Positive references to relations are well formed in binding Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} according to PP-PosAtom when (a) the use is well typed (p⊆τi→∈Φp\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}\in\Phi) and (b) the variables used in the premise yield the binding Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}. Negative references to relations !​p​(Xi→)\mathord{!}p(\vec{X_{i}}) additionally require that all of the XiX_{i} be already bound, i.e., the resulting Γ\Gamma is the same as the starting one. We split expression equality constraints Y=eY=e into three main cases:

  1. (1)

    YY is bound and ee is a constructor c⁡(Xi→)c(\vec{X_{i}}) where all of Xi→\vec{X_{i}} are unbound (PP-EqCtor-BF).

  2. (2)

    YY is bound and ee is a quoted SMT constructor `​c𝖼′𝖲𝖬𝖳​(,​Xi→)​`\textsf{\`{}}{c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{c^{\prime}}}(\vec{\textbf{,}{X_{i}}})}\textsf{\`{}} where all of Xi→\vec{X_{i}} are unbound (PP-EqSMT-BF).

  3. (3)

    YY is possibly unbound and ee has no unbound variables (PP-Eq-FB).

It is critical that we avoid the case where both YY and some of the XiX_{i} are unbound, in which case we would need to perform true unification (or even higher-order unification, depending on our treatment of functional programs). In the case where YY is bound and the expression has no unbound variables, only the PP-Eq-FB case could apply. There is a fourth, irrelevant case: PP-NegEq. No binding can possibly occur there, so the constraint is imply checked by running ee and making sure it isn’t equal to YY.

The binding rules come in three forms: X​τX\tau-Bind for adding a new binding, X​τX\tau-Check for ensuring that an already bound variable is matched at appropriate type, and a vectorized form X→​τ→\vec{X}\vec{\tau}-All for folding over a sequence of such bindings. Note that the resulting bindings are the same, i.e., Γ⊢X,τ⊳Γ\Gamma\vdash X,\tau\rhd\Gamma, if and only if X∈dom⁡(Γ)X\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma); the same holds for vectors of variables and types, as well (Lemma E.5).

We split the rules for expressions ee and formulas ϕ\phi in two parts (Figures 18 and 19, respectively). Expression typing is conventional for functional languages. We adopt a declarative style for type substitutions (ee-Ctor, ee-Fun, ee-Op, ee-Match). Our actual implementation uses Hindley–Damas–Milner type inference (Hindley, 1969; Damas and Milner, 1982) to find the correct types to use. As to Formulog-specific features, we ensure type well formedness is in 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}-mode; the `​ϕ​`\textsf{\`{}}{\phi}\textsf{\`{}} expression switches from expression mode to formula mode. Relations p⊆τi→∈Φp\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}\in\Phi are treated as if they are functions of type τi→→𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\mathsf{bool}. Since Datalog predicates can occur in functional terms, we must use the control-flow graph of the program when analyzing for stratification. Consider the following program:

⬇
fun f(X : bv[32]) : bv[32] = if p(X) then ... else X
p(Y) :- q(Y, Y).
q(A, B) :- r(A), B = f(A).
r(42).

Here the relation q calls the function f, which in turn relies on the negation of the relation p (since the behavior of f is conditioned on the contents of p). As p is defined in terms of q, this leads to a circularity we want to avoid: It is possible to derive q(42,42), but this derivation nonsensically relies on q(42, 42) being false (since it requires that p(42) is false).

While Formulog’s expressions compute values, the Formulog’s formulas construct ASTs, to be shipped off to an SMT solver. Our formal account here uniformly uses SMT constructors to model the SMT syntax, but our implementation offers special-purpose syntax. For example, we write c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,\mathsf{bv[32]}] in our formalism to name a 32-bit integer variable xx, while in our implementation one might write \#x[bv[32]].

Every ϕ\phi-…\dots typing rule generates a value with an SMT type, i.e., either t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} or t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} for SMT types tt, i.e., Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t (Lemma D.9). The cc-SMT-* rules yield t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} and t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt}. SMT variables c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,t]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,t] are written in lowercase to emphasize their distinction from expression variables XX; these SMT variables will be used as names in the formulas sent to the SMT solver. We keep track of which terms are SMT variables c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,t]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,t] of type t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} (generated by cc-SMT-Var) and which are plain SMT formulas of type t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} (all other rules). We treat t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} as a subtype of t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} (ϕ\phi-Promote).

The `​ϕ​`\textsf{\`{}}{\phi}\textsf{\`{}} operator is an expression term that introduces quoted SMT formulas represented as special, SMT constructors of the form c𝖲𝖬𝖳...c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{...}} (described below); the ,​e\textbf{,}{e} operator is the corresponding ‘unquote’ operator that introduces an expression (ϕ\phi-Unquote).

While unquoting generally suffices for embedding the results of expressions in formulas, we treat constructors specially so that we can mix concrete and symbolic (i.e., SMT) arguments in a single data type constructor (cc-SMT-Ctor): we assign them types that are fully SMT-ized via the toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} function, but unquoting allows for easy mixing of values of SMT-types tt as if they were of type t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt}. The toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} metafunction alters the type of ee to make sure it is SMT representable; toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} relies on an erase\mathrm{erase} function to avoid nesting …​𝗌𝗆𝗍{\dots}~\mathsf{smt} and …​𝗌𝗒𝗆{\dots}~\mathsf{sym} type constructors. One can only run these functions on SMT types. For example, we can write terms like the following in concrete syntax:

𝗅𝖾𝗍​H=5​𝗂𝗇​`​𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌​(H,#​l​[𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]​𝗅𝗂𝗌𝗍])​`\mathsf{let}~{H}={5}~\mathsf{in}~{\textsf{\`{}}{\mathsf{cons}(H,\#l[\mathsf{bv[32]}~\mathsf{list}])}\textsf{\`{}}}

which desugars to the SMT constructors:

𝗅𝖾𝗍​H=5​𝗂𝗇​`​c𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌]​(,​H,c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[l,𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]​𝗅𝗂𝗌𝗍]​())​`\mathsf{let}~{H}={5}~\mathsf{in}~{\textsf{\`{}}{c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{ctor}}[\mathsf{cons}](\textbf{,}{H},c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[l,\mathsf{bv[32]}~\mathsf{list}]())}\textsf{\`{}}}

Note that HH is an expression variable and ll is an SMT variable; the type conversion in ϕ\phi-Unquote lets us mix them in the same list of 32-bit numbers. The t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} type is used in ϕ\phi-Let and ϕ\phi-Forall, which construct SMT formuale that use binders. The only way to get a value of type t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym} is either with cc-SMT-Var/ϕ\phi-Ctor or with ϕ\phi-Unquote, as in 𝗅𝖾𝗍​X=`​c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]]​`​𝗂𝗇​`,​X​`\mathsf{let}~{X}={\textsf{\`{}}{c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,\mathsf{bv[32]}]}\textsf{\`{}}}~\mathsf{in}~{\textsf{\`{}}{\textbf{,}{X}}\textsf{\`{}}}.

Uninterpreted functions must be applied to appropriate SMT types (ϕ\phi-UFun); recall that Φ\Phi-UFun ensures that each uninterpreted function’s types are SMT representable.

Finally, there are a suite of SMT constructors of the form c…𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{\dots}}. Each of these special c…𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{\dots}} constructors is treated as an ordinary constructor by the operational semantics, even though the constructors don’t appear in Δ\Delta. Rather than making SMT terms opaque, we model them with constructors to allow for matching on generated formulae in PP-EqSMT-BF and PP-Eq-FB. The types of the SMT constructors c…𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{\dots}} are given in Figure 19. It is a crucial invariant that all of these types be SMT types: we would not want to treat an SMT variable c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,\mathsf{bool}] as though it were an actual 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool}! Reusing the cc-SMT-…\dots rules is convenient—we need only state the types of these constructors once and we get precise types in our premises. Several SMT constructors take special arguments in square brackets: c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,t]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,t] is a 0-ary SMT constructor, while c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}} itself is a family of SMT constructors for given variable names xx and pre-types tt; similarly, c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳​[k]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}}[k] is a 0-ary SMT constructor, while c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}} itself is a family of SMT constructors for given constants kk. The embedding of data type constructors c𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[c]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{ctor}}[c] is similarly parameterized on a constructor name cc, and the embedding of uninterpreted functions c𝗎𝖿𝖲𝖬𝖳​[𝑢𝑓]c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{uf}}[\mathit{uf}] takes an uninterpereted function as a parameter. Separating these parameters from the interesting, ϕ\phi-shaped subparts of each SMT constructor lets us reuse the cc-SMT-…\dots rules when typing premises that might bind to subparts of an SMT formula (PP-EqSMT-…\dots, Figure 17).

Our formal model elides some of the detail of our SMT encoding, such as constructors for SMT operations like bit vector manipulation or equality. These operations are all encoded as more SMT-specific constructors, i.e., OPENc𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[𝖻𝗏𝟥𝟤​_​𝖺𝖽𝖽]​(c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,𝖻𝗏⁡[𝟥𝟤]],c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳​[1]))c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{ctor}}[\mathsf{bv_{32}\_add}](c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,\mathsf{bv[32]}],c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}}[1])) represents result of adding the 32-bit vector xx and 11. There are some subtle issues around polymorphism and determinacy. We give a monomorphic interpretation of SMT here, though our SMT constructors can work with our polymorphic data types. Our implementation treats equality and other polymorphic SMT operations specially, where each use of a polymorphic operator must be fully instantiated. In practice our implementation can usually infer the instantiation; users must annotate in those places we cannot infer.

Appendix C Operational semantics

Formulog’s operational semantics operates over worlds 𝒲\mathcal{W} and substitutions θ\theta (Figure 20); the semantics is a mix of small-step rules modeling a single application of a Datalog rule (Figure 21), which depend on a small-step rules explaining how premises unify (Figures 22 and 23); the premise semantics in turn depends on a semantics of expressions (Figures 24 and 25) and formulas (Figure 26).

Our worlds 𝒲\mathcal{W} are (subsets of) Herbrand models. Our small-step semantics iteratively builds up a world that is in fact a Herbrand model of the original relations in the program. We could have modeled our semi-naive evaluation model for Formulog in more detail, showing that all programs generate a world 𝒲\mathcal{W} that is a well typed Herbrand model of the user’s program (possibly taking infinite time to do so). Doing so wouldn’t add anything materially interesting to our formulation.

Throughout, the type system’s goal is prevent a program yielding ⊥\bot, the bottom “wrong” value. Such a value denotes a serious, unrecoverable error, such as using a relation with the wrong arity or conditioning on a non-boolean. It is important to distinguish bad, ⊥\bot-yielding programs from those that simply fail to step. The goal of Datalog evaluation is to reach a fixed point, i.e., to be unable to step! Finally, as is common, we assume that built-in operations do not yield ⊥\bot, i.e., they are total. While we could in principle design a type system for Formulog that avoids, say, division by zero, we are more interested in making the hard parts easy (generating well typed SMT formulas) rather than making the easy parts foolproof (statically protecting partial functions).

Rules of the form …\dots-Enn denote ⊥\bot-yielding rules. Each such rule characterizes a form of wrongness avoided by our static type system. We write v⊥v_{\bot} to denote the disjoint sum of values vv and the wrong value ⊥\bot.

During correct execution, Clause takes a Horn clause p⁡(Xj→):​-Pi→p(\vec{X_{j}})\mathrel{\mathsf{\mathord{:}\mathord{-}}}\vec{P_{i}}, executes each premise PiP_{i} from left to right, yielding a final substitution for the variables Xj→\vec{X_{j}} in the head of the rule. There are two possible failing rules. Clause-E1 simply propagates the first error from a premise; Clause-E2 fails because not every XjX_{j} in the head of the rule is bound by the end. Since Formulog enforces the range restriction (HH-Clause), Clause-E2 can never apply in a well typed program. Finally, the Clause* operational rules and the HH-Clause typing rule both use the fixed, given order of premises for checking. Different orderings induce different binding orders, some of which may succeed and some of which may not.

The premise semantics (Figure 22) uses unification (Figure 23) to match and bind variables. Positive atoms p⁡(Xi→)p(\vec{X_{i}}) try to unify their arguments with a tuple for pp drawn from the world 𝒲\mathcal{W} (PosAtom). Negative atoms p⁡(Xi→)p(\vec{X_{i}}) require that all of their arguments XiX_{i} are already bound (NegAtom); failing to find such bound terms yields an error (NegAtom-E). Rules for equations also use unification, whether for a constructor over variables (EqCtor) or an expression (EqExpr). The latter can fail if evaluation fails (EqExpr-E). Before discussing term evaluation, we give rules for unification.

Unification is split into two levels. Unification proper takes a pair of unifiable terms—values with variables in them—and tries to yield a substitution. Value unification takes a unifiable term and a value and tries to yield a substitution. The unification rules are of the form u​uuu-…\dots. These rules analyze the two unifiable terms to find which side is completely bound—i.e., applying θ\theta can completely fill in the variables—and so can be passed to value unification as a value. The B and F in these rules stand for Bound and Free. The only error in unification is in u​uuu-FF, when neither unifiable term is bound to a value. We write a case for when both unifiable terms are bound (u​uuu-BB) and require that they are directly equal—but it would also work to drop this rule and rely on value unification to identify the equality.

Value unification rules are of the form u​vuv-…\dots. The rules here lookup variables in the unifiable term and either check that the binding conforms to the given value (u​vuv-Eq-Var, cf. X​τX\tau-Check) or binds the value (u​vuv-Bind-Var, cf. X​τX\tau-Bind). The remaining value unification rules match the structure of the unifiable term to the structure of the value (u​vuv-Constant, u​vuv-Ctor) or fold value unification along a vector (u→​v→\vec{u}\vec{v}-All). Value unification never produces ⊥\bot. It isn’t an error when two values fail to unify, since one might have to search through many tuples for a relation in 𝒲\mathcal{W} to find a one that matches, say, a given constructor.

The expression semantics is an entirely conventional big-step semantics using explicit substitutions. The operational rules implicitly take the function definitions F→\vec{F} for use in applications (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun).

There are a variety of wrong behaviors prevented by our type system, mostly concerning mismatches between values and elimination forms: unbound variables (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Var-E); mistyped arguments to built-in operations (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Op-E2); function, relation and constructor arity errors (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun-E2, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-E2, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Match-E4); non-existent functions and relations (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun-E3, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-E3); conditionals on inappropriate values (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Match-E2, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Ite-E2); and ill formed constructor names (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Match-E3); The remaining rules propagate errors (⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Let-E, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Op-E1, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun-E1, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-E1, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Match-E1, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Ite-E1). As mentioned in the early discussion of our semantics in this section, ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Op-E2 is not about division by zero (a form of going wrong our type system doesn’t prevent), but about mis-application of built-in functions, e.g., taking the boolean negation of a number.

The operational semantics on formulas is simple: the rules generate ASTs for the SMT solver using the c…𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{\dots}} constructors: constants (c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}}), SMT variables (c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}), SMT data types (c𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{ctor}}), let bindings (c𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{let}}), quantification (c𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{forall}}), and uninterpreted function application (c𝗎𝖿𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{uf}}).

When unquoting values resulting from evaluating expressions, we use the toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} function to translate expression values into the SMT’s AST. The toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} function is an identity on SMT ASTs, but it explicitly tags the constants and Formulog-defined constructors using c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}} and c𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{ctor}}.

Appendix D Metatheory

We break the metatheory into two parts: lemmas characterizing the SMT conversion (Section D.1) and lemmas showing type safety (Section E). The SMT lemmas culminate in two proofs: first, regularity (Lemma D.9) guarantees that (a) every type or context generated by the operational semantics is well formed and (b) that formula evaluation generates well typed SMT ASTs; second, we show that SMT conversion of values agrees with SMT conversion of types (Lemma D.10). Type safety culminates in theorems showing that premises don’t yield ⊥\bot and generate well typed substitutions (Lemma E.4) and so Horn clauses (a) never yield ⊥\bot (Theorem E.6) and (b) take well typed worlds to well typed worlds (Theorem E.7).

D.1. SMT Conversion

We show a variety of properties of the erasure and SMT conversion functions: 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt} is a sub-kind of 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp} (Lemma D.1); erasures and SMT conversion yield well formed types from SMT types (Lemmas D.2, D.3, D.4, and D.5); weakening and strengthening of typing contexts (Lemmas D.6 and D.7); type variable substitution (Lemma D.8)—we have no need of a value substitution lemma because our semantics uses environments; regularity (Lemma D.9); and, finally, that SMT conversion of values agrees with SMT conversion of types (Lemma D.10).

Lemma D.1 (𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt} is a subkind of 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}).

If Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau then Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau.

Proof.

By induction on τ\tau.

  • (τ=B\tau=B)

    Immediate: τ\tau-Base allows any mm.

  • (τ=α\tau=\alpha)

    Contradictory—type variables are only well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}.

  • (τ=D​τi→\tau=D~\vec{\tau_{i}})

    By the IH on each τi\tau_{i} and tt-ADT.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt})

    Immediate: τ\tau-SMT allows any mm.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t}~\mathsf{sym})

    Immediate: τ\tau-SMT allows any mm.

  • (τ=𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\tau=\mathsf{model})

    Contradictory—𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} is only well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}. ∎

Lemma D.2 (Erasure is well formed).

If Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau then Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍erase(τ)\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{erase}(\tau).

Proof.

By induction on the well formedness derivation.

  • (tt-Base)

    Immediate, since erase⁡(B)=B\mathrm{erase}(B)=B.

  • (tt-TVar)

    Contradictory—type variables aren’t well typed at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}.

  • (tt-ADT)

    By the IH on each constituent of D​τi→D~\vec{\tau_{i}}, and then by tt-ADT.

  • (τ\tau-SMT)

    Since erase⁡(t​𝗌𝗆𝗍)=erase⁡(t)\mathrm{erase}({t}~\mathsf{smt})=\mathrm{erase}(t), by the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t.

  • (τ\tau-Sym)

    Since erase⁡(t​𝗌𝗒𝗆)=erase⁡(t)\mathrm{erase}({t}~\mathsf{sym})=\mathrm{erase}(t), by the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t.

  • (τ\tau-Model)

    Contradictory—𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} isn’t well typed at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}. ∎

Lemma D.3 (SMT types have only SMT parts).

If Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau, then all of τ\tau’s subparts are also well formed at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}.

Proof.

By induction on τ\tau.

  • (τ=B\tau=B)

    Immediate.

  • (τ=α\tau=\alpha)

    Contradictory—type variables are only well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}.

  • (τ=D​τi→\tau=D~\vec{\tau_{i}})

    By the IH on each τi\tau_{i}.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt})

    By the IH on tt.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t}~\mathsf{sym})

    By the IH on tt.

  • (τ=𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\tau=\mathsf{model})

    Contradictory—𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} is only well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}. ∎

Lemma D.4 (SMT conversion is well formed).

If Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau then toSMT⁡(τ)=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau)={t}~\mathsf{sym} or t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} such that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t (and so Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍toSMT(τ)\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau)).

Proof.

By induction on the well formedness derivation.

  • (tt-Base)

    toSMT⁡(B)=B​𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathrm{toSMT}(B)={B}~\mathsf{smt}, which is well formed by τ\tau-SMT and tt-B.

  • (tt-TVar)

    Contradictory—type variables are only well formed at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}.

  • (tt-ADT)

    We know that erase⁡(D​τi→)\mathrm{erase}(D~\vec{\tau_{i}}) is still well formed by Lemma D.2; then by τ\tau-SMT.

  • (τ\tau-SMT)

    Since it must be that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t, then erase⁡(t)\mathrm{erase}(t) is also well formed by Lemma D.2; then by τ\tau-SMT.

  • (τ\tau-Sym)

    Since it must be that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t, then erase⁡(t)\mathrm{erase}(t) is also well formed by Lemma D.2; then by τ\tau-Sym.

  • (τ\tau-Model)

    Contradictory—𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} is only well formed at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt} ∎

Lemma D.5 (SMT conversion is only for SMT types).

toSMT⁡(τ)\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau) is defined iff Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau.

Proof.

The right-to-left direction is proved by Lemma D.4. For left-to-right, we go by induction on τ\tau.

  • (τ=B\tau=B)

    By tt-Base.

  • (τ=α\tau=\alpha)

    Contradictory—type variables are undefined for erase\mathrm{erase}.

  • (τ=D​τi→\tau=D~\vec{\tau_{i}})

    By the IH on each τi\tau_{i} and tt-ADT.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt})

    By the IH on tt and τ\tau-SMT.

  • (τ=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t}~\mathsf{sym})

    By the IH on tt and τ\tau-Sym.

  • (τ=𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\tau=\mathsf{model})

    Contradictory—𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} is undefined for erase\mathrm{erase}. ∎

We say a type tt is an “SMT type” when Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t; a type τ\tau is an SMT type when it is equal to an SMT type tt or when it is of the form t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} or t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym}. Note that toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} always produces an SMT type, but does not work on types that contain type variables or the unrepresentable 𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅\mathsf{model} type.

Lemma D.6 (Weakening).

If ⊢Γ\vdash\Gamma and ⊢Γ′\vdash\Gamma^{\prime} and dom⁡(Γ)∩dom⁡(Γ′)=∅\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma)\cap\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma^{\prime})=\emptyset then:

  1. (1)

    ⊢Γ,Γ′\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}

  2. (2)

    If Γ⊢mτ\Gamma\vdash_{m}\tau then Γ,Γ′⊢mτ\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash_{m}\tau;

  3. (3)

    If Γ⊢e:τ\Gamma\vdash e:\tau then Γ,Γ′⊢e:τ\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash e:\tau; and

  4. (4)

    If Γ⊢ϕ:τ\Gamma\vdash\phi:\tau then Γ,Γ′⊢ϕ:τ\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash\phi:\tau.

Proof.

By mutual induction on the derivations.

Contexts
  • (Γ\Gamma-Empty)

    We have Γ′=⋅\Gamma^{\prime}=\cdot; immediate by assumption.

  • (Γ\Gamma-Var)

    We have Γ′=Γ′′,X:τ\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma^{\prime\prime},X:\tau. By the IH on Γ′′\Gamma^{\prime\prime} and Γ\Gamma-Var, finding Γ,Γ′′⊢mτ\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime\prime}\vdash_{m}\tau by part (2) of the IH.

  • (Γ\Gamma-TVar)

    We have Γ′=Γ′′,α\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma^{\prime\prime},\alpha. By the IH on Γ′′\Gamma^{\prime\prime} and Γ\Gamma-TVar.

Type well formedness
  • (tt-Base)

    Immediate, by tt-Base.

  • (tt-TVar)

    Since Γ\Gamma and Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} have disjoint domains, we know α∈Γ\alpha\in\Gamma—by tt-TVar.

  • (tt-ADT)

    By the IH on each constituent of D​τi→D~\vec{\tau_{i}}, followed by tt-ADT.

  • (τ\tau-SMT)

    By the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t and then τ\tau-SMT.

  • (τ\tau-Sym)

    By the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t and then τ\tau-Sym.

  • (τ\tau-Model)

    Immediate, by τ\tau-Model. ∎

Expressions
  • (ee-Var)

    Since the domains are disjoint, (Γ,Γ′)​(X)=τ(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime})(X)=\tau and we can still find ee-Var.

  • (ee-Const)

    Immediate, by ee-Const.

  • (ee-Let)

    By the ee-Let and the IH on e1e_{1} and e2e_{2}, α\alpha-renaming XX appropriately.

  • (ee-Ctor)

    By ee-Ctor and the IH, using part (2) on τj′\tau_{j}^{\prime} and part (3) on eie_{i}.

  • (ee-Quote)

    By the part (4) of the IH.

  • (ee-Rel)

    By ee-Rel and the IH on each eie_{i}.

  • (ee-Fun)

    By ee-Fun and the the IH, using part (2) on τj′\tau_{j}^{\prime} and part (3) on eie_{i}.

  • (ee-Op)

    By ee-Op and the the IH, using part (2) on τj′\tau_{j}^{\prime} and part (3) on eie_{i}.

  • (ee-If)

    By ee-If and the IH on each of the eie_{i}.

  • (ee-Match)

    By ee-Match and the IH on ee and each of the eie_{i}, α\alpha-renaming each XkX_{k} appropriately.

Formulas
  • (ϕ\phi-Var)

    By ϕ\phi-Var and part (2) of the IH.

  • (ϕ\phi-Promote)

    By ϕ\phi-Promote and the IH.

  • (ϕ\phi-Unquote)

    By ϕ\phi-Unquote and part (3) of the IH.

  • (ϕ\phi-Ctor)

    By ϕ\phi-Ctor and the IH, using part (2) on the τi\tau_{i} and part (4) on ϕi\phi_{i}, observing that the actual types are unchanged, and so the toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} conversions are the same.

Lemma D.7 (Type well formedness strengthening).

If Γ,X:τ,Γ′⊢mτ′\Gamma,X:\tau,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash_{m}\tau^{\prime} then Γ,Γ′⊢τ′\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash\tau^{\prime}.

Proof.
  • (tt-Base)

    Immediate.

  • (tt-TVar)

    Immediate: removing the variable binding can’t affect α\alpha.

  • (tt-ADT)

    By the IH on each constituent of D​τi→D~\vec{\tau_{i}}.

  • (τ\tau-SMT)

    By the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t.

  • (τ\tau-Sym)

    By the IH on Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t.

  • (τ\tau-Model)

    Immediate. ∎

Lemma D.8 (Type variable substitution).

If ⊢Γ,α,Γ′\vdash\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime} and Γ⊢mτ′\Gamma\vdash_{m}\tau^{\prime}, then:

  1. (1)

    ⊢Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha];

  2. (2)

    If Γ,α,Γ′⊢mτ\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash_{m}\tau then Γ,Γ′[τ/α]⊢mτ′[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash_{m}\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha];

  3. (3)

    If Γ,α,Γ′⊢X,τ′⊳Γ′′\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}\rhd\Gamma^{\prime\prime} then Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢X,τ′​[τ/α]⊳Γ′′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\rhd\Gamma^{\prime\prime}[\tau/\alpha]; and

  4. (4)

    If Γ,α,Γ′⊢Xi→,τi′→⊳Γ′′\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau^{\prime}_{i}}\rhd\Gamma^{\prime\prime} then Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢Xi→,τi′→​[τ/α]⊳Γ′′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau^{\prime}_{i}}[\tau/\alpha]\rhd\Gamma^{\prime\prime}[\tau/\alpha].

Proof.

For parts (1) and (2), by mutual induction on the derivations. Note that if α\alpha actually occurs in the type, we could only have found well formedness at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp}.

  • (Γ\Gamma-Empty)

    Contradictory: ⋅≠Γ,α,Γ′\cdot\neq\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}.

  • (Γ\Gamma-Var)

    We have Γ′=Γ′′,X:τ′\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma^{\prime\prime},X:\tau^{\prime} where Γ,Γ′′⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ′\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime\prime}\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau^{\prime}. By the IH on Γ′′\Gamma^{\prime\prime}, we know that ⊢Γ,Γ′′​[τ/α]\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime\prime}[\tau/\alpha]; by part (2), we have Γ,Γ′′[τ/α]⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ′[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]; and so we have ⊢Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha] by Γ\Gamma-Var.

  • (Γ\Gamma-TVar)

    We have Γ′=Γ′′,β\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma^{\prime\prime},\beta; by the IH on Γ′′\Gamma^{\prime\prime}, we have ⊢Γ,Γ′′​[τ/α]\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime\prime}[\tau/\alpha]; since β⁡[τ/α]=β\beta[\tau/\alpha]=\beta, we can apply Γ\Gamma-TVar to find ⊢Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\vdash\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha] as desired.

  • (tt-B)

    Immediate by tt-B, since B⁡[τ/α]=BB[\tau/\alpha]=B.

  • (tt-TVar)

    We have τ′=β\tau^{\prime}=\beta. If α=β\alpha=\beta, then we have Γ⊢mα[τ/α]\Gamma\vdash_{m}\alpha[\tau/\alpha] by assumption. If α≠β\alpha\neq\beta, then it must be that β∈Γ\beta\in\Gamma or Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}—either way, β\beta is unaffected by the substitution and we have β∈Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\beta\in\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha] and so Γ,Γ′[τ/α]⊢mβ\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash_{m}\beta by tt-TVar.

  • (tt-ADT)

    By the IH on each premise, followed by tt-ADT.

  • (τ\tau-SMT)

    By the IH on Γ,α,Γ′⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t and then by τ\tau-SMT.

  • (τ\tau-Sym)

    By the IH on Γ,α,Γ′⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t and then by τ\tau-Sym.

  • (τ\tau-Model)

    Immediate by τ\tau-Model.

For parts (3) and (4), by mutual induction on the derivations.

  • (X​τX\tau-Bind)

    We have X∉dom⁡(Γ,α,Γ′)X\not\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime}), so it must also be the case that X∉dom⁡(Γ,Γ′​[τ/α])X\not\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]). We therefore find Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢X,τ′​[τ/α]⊳Γ,Γ′​[τ/α],τ′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\rhd\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha],\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha] by X​τX\tau-Bind.

  • (X​τX\tau-Check)

    We have (Γ,α,Γ′)​(X)=τ′(\Gamma,\alpha,\Gamma^{\prime})(X)=\tau^{\prime}. Is X:τ′X:\tau^{\prime} in Γ\Gamma or Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}? Either way we will find Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢X,τ′​[τ/α]⊳Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\rhd\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha] by X​τX\tau-Check.

    If τ′∈dom⁡(Γ)\tau^{\prime}\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma), then Γ⊢τ′\Gamma\vdash\tau^{\prime} and so τ′​[τ/α]=τ′\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]=\tau^{\prime} (Γ,Γ′​[τ/α])​(X)=τ′(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha])(X)=\tau^{\prime} and we have Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢X,τ′⊳Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}\rhd\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha].

    If, on the other hand, τ′∈dom⁡(Γ′)\tau^{\prime}\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma^{\prime}), then (Γ,Γ′​[τ/α])​(X)=τ′​[τ/α](\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha])(X)=\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]. We therefore have Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]⊢X,τ′​[τ/α]⊳Γ,Γ′​[τ/α]\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\vdash X,\tau^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha]\rhd\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}[\tau/\alpha].

  • (X→​τ→\vec{X}\vec{\tau}-All)

    By part (3) of the IH on each premise. ∎

Lemma D.9 (Regularity; formulas have SMT types).
  1. (1)

    If ⊢Γ\vdash\Gamma and Γ⁡(X)=τ\Gamma(X)=\tau then Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau.

  2. (2)

    If ⊢Φ\vdash\Phi then (a) if f:∀αj→,τi→→τ∈Φf:\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\tau\in\Phi then αj→⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\vec{\alpha_{j}}\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau, and (b) if 𝑢𝑓:ti′→→t∈Φ\mathit{uf}:\vec{t_{i}^{\prime}}\rightarrow t\in\Phi then ⋅⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\cdot\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t.

  3. (3)

    If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢e:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash e:\tau then Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau.

  4. (4)

    If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢c𝖼𝖲𝖬𝖳​(ϕi→):τi→→τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{c}}(\vec{\phi_{i}}):\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\tau then τi=ti​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau_{i}={t_{i}}~\mathsf{smt} or τi=ti​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau_{i}={t_{i}}~\mathsf{sym} and τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt} or τ=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t}~\mathsf{sym} and Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τi\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau_{i} and Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau.

  5. (5)

    If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ϕ:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\phi:\tau then τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt} or τ=t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t}~\mathsf{sym} and Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau.

  6. (6)

    If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ei→:τi→\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\vec{e_{i}}:\vec{\tau_{i}} then Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τi\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{i}.

  7. (7)

    If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ϕi→:τi→\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\vec{\phi_{i}}:\vec{\tau_{i}} then τi=ti​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau_{i}={t_{i}}~\mathsf{smt} or τ=ti​𝗌𝗒𝗆\tau={t_{i}}~\mathsf{sym} and Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍ti\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t_{i} (and so Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τi\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{i}).

Proof.

By induction on the typing derivation.

Contexts
  • (Γ\Gamma-Empty)

    Contradictory—there’s no way ⋅\cdot has a binding for XX.

  • (Γ\Gamma-Var)

    Γ=Γ′,Y:τ\Gamma=\Gamma^{\prime},Y:\tau. If X=YX=Y, then we know Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau by assumption; otherwise, by the IH on Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}.

  • (Γ\Gamma-TVar)

    Γ=Γ′,α\Gamma=\Gamma^{\prime},\alpha. By the IH on Γ\Gamma.

Program signatures
  • (Φ\Phi-Empty)

    Contradictory—there are no function definitions in ⋅\cdot.

  • (Φ\Phi-Fun)

    Φ=Φ′,g:…\Phi=\Phi^{\prime},g:\dots. For case (a) when f=gf=g, then by assumption. Otherwise, by the IH on Φ′\Phi^{\prime}.

  • (Φ\Phi-Rel)

    Φ=Φ′,p⊆τi→\Phi=\Phi^{\prime},p\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}. By the IH on Φ\Phi.

  • (Φ\Phi-UFun)

    Φ=Φ′,𝑢𝑓′:ti′→→t\Phi=\Phi^{\prime},\mathit{uf}^{\prime}:\vec{t_{i}^{\prime}}\rightarrow t. For case (b) when 𝑢𝑓=𝑢𝑓′\mathit{uf}=\mathit{uf}^{\prime}, then by assumption. Otherwise, by the IH on Φ′\Phi^{\prime}.

Expressions
  • (ee-Var)

    By the part (1) on ⊢Γ\vdash\Gamma.

  • (ee-Const)

    By assumption, we know that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍typeof(k)\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{typeof}(k); by Lemma D.1 we can find Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉typeof(k)\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\mathrm{typeof}(k).

  • (ee-Let)

    By the IH on Γ,X:τ1⊢e2:τ2\Gamma,X:\tau_{1}\vdash e_{2}:\tau_{2}, using strengthening (Lemma D.7) to find that if Γ,X:τ1⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ2\Gamma,X:\tau_{1}\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{2} then Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ2\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{2}.

  • (ee-Ctor)

    Since Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τj′\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{j}^{\prime}, we know by tt-ADT that Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉Dτj′→\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}D~\vec{\tau_{j}^{\prime}}.

  • (ee-Quote)

    By the IH on part (5), we know that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau (and, less relevantly, that τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt} or t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym}). We can find the same well formedness at 𝖾𝗑𝗉\mathsf{exp} by Lemma D.1.

  • (ee-Rel)

    Immediate by tt-B.

  • (ee-Fun)

    Since f:∀αj→,τi→→τ∈Φf:\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\tau\in\Phi and ⊢Φ\vdash\Phi, we know by part (2) of the IH know that αj→⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\vec{\alpha_{j}}\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau. By weakening (Lemma D.6) we can lift that well formedness judgment to Γ\Gamma. Since each Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τj′\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{j}^{\prime}, we can find that Γ⊢τ⁡[τj′/αj]\Gamma\vdash\tau[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}] by substitution (Lemma D.8).

  • (ee-Fun)

    We have by assumption that typeof⁡(⊗)\mathrm{typeof}(\otimes) yields a well-formed type, i.e., αj→⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\vec{\alpha_{j}}\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau (and also for each τi\tau_{i}). By weakening (Lemma D.6) we can lift that well formedness judgment to Γ\Gamma. Since each Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τj′\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{j}^{\prime}, we can find that Γ⊢τ⁡[τj′/αj]\Gamma\vdash\tau[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}] by substitution (Lemma D.8).

  • (ee-If)

    By the IH on Γ⊢e2:t\Gamma\vdash e_{2}:t.

  • (ee-Match)

    By the IH on Γ,X1:τ1​[τj/αj]→⊢e1:τ\Gamma,\overrightarrow{X_{1}:\tau_{1}[\tau_{j}/\alpha_{j}]}\vdash e_{1}:\tau we have Γ,X1:τ1​[τj/αj]→⊢τ\Gamma,\overrightarrow{X_{1}:\tau_{1}[\tau_{j}/\alpha_{j}]}\vdash\tau; we can use strengthening (Lemma D.7) to find Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau.

SMT constructors
  • (cc-SMT-Var)

    Immediate, with Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t coming from the rule itself.

  • (cc-SMT-Const)

    Immediate, since we have by assumption that ⋅⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍typeof(k)\cdot\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{typeof}(k).

  • (cc-SMT-Let)

    Immediate, with the necessary well formedness assumptions coming from the rule itself.

  • (cc-SMT-Ctor)

    We know that D​tj′→D~\vec{t_{j}^{\prime}} is well formed by tt-ADT. We can find the translation of the argument types well formed by Lemma D.4 on each of the Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τi[tj′/αj]\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau_{i}[t_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}] derivations.

  • (cc-SMT-Forall)

    Immediate, with the necessary Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t1\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t_{1} coming from the rule itself.

  • (cc-SMT-UFun)

    Since ⊢Φ\vdash\Phi and 𝑢𝑓:ti→→t∈Φ\mathit{uf}:\vec{t_{i}}\rightarrow t\in\Phi, we know that ⋅⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\cdot\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t by part (2) of the IH and so ⋅⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t𝗌𝗆𝗍\cdot\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}{t}~\mathsf{smt}, which we can lift to Γ\Gamma by weakening (Lemma D.6).

Formulas
  • (ϕ\phi-Promote)

    Since Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ϕ:t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\phi:{t}~\mathsf{sym}, we know that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍t\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}t and so we are correct in yielding τ=t​𝗌𝗆𝗍\tau={t}~\mathsf{smt}.

  • (ϕ\phi-Unquote)

    We have Δ;Φ;Γ⊢e:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash e:\tau such that Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau. By Lemma D.4 we know that toSMT⁡(τ)\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau) is a well formed SMT type.

  • (ϕ\phi-Ctor)

    By the IH part (4) on Γ⊢c𝖼𝖲𝖬𝖳:τi→→τ\Gamma\vdash c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{c}}:\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\tau.

Vectored expressions and formulas

By the IH for parts (3) and (5), respectively.

∎

Lemma D.10 (SMT value conversion is type correct).

If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢v:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash v:\tau and Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍τ\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\tau then Δ;Φ;Γ⊢toSMT⁡(v):toSMT⁡(τ)\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\mathrm{toSMT}(v):\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau).

Proof.

First, observe that τ\tau and all of its parts must be well formed at 𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathsf{smt}, by Lemmas D.5 and D.3. By induction on the typing derivation. In expression mode, the applicable rules are ee-Const and ee-Ctor; only a few typing rules could even have applied to a value in formula mode: the ϕ\phi-Ctor and ϕ\phi-Promote.

  • (ee-Const)

    We have Γ⊢k:typeof⁡(k)\Gamma\vdash k:\mathrm{typeof}(k); since toSMT⁡(k)=c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳​[k]​()\mathrm{toSMT}(k)=c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}}[k]() and toSMT⁡(typeof⁡(k))=k​𝗌𝗆𝗍\mathrm{toSMT}(\mathrm{typeof}(k))={k}~\mathsf{smt} (since Γ⊢𝗌𝗆𝗍typeof(k)\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{smt}}\mathrm{typeof}(k) by assumption), we must show that Γ⊢c𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍𝖲𝖬𝖳​[k]​():typeof⁡(k)​𝗌𝗆𝗍\Gamma\vdash c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{const}}[k]():{\mathrm{typeof}(k)}~\mathsf{smt}, which we have by ϕ\phi-SMT-Const.

    We have v=c⁡(vi→)v=c(\vec{v_{i}}) and:

    Δ(D)=∀αj→,{…,c:τi→,…}Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝗉τj′Γ⊢vi:τi[τj′/αj]\Delta(D)=\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\{\dots,c:\vec{\tau_{i}},\dots\}\quad\quad\Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{exp}}\tau_{j}^{\prime}\quad\quad\Gamma\vdash v_{i}:\tau_{i}[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}]

By the IH on each of these viv_{i}, we know that we find appropriate values at appropriately converted types, i.e., Γ⊢toSMT⁡(vi):toSMT⁡(τi​[τj′/αj])\Gamma\vdash\mathrm{toSMT}(v_{i}):\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau_{i}[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}]). By Lemma D.4, we know toSMT⁡(τi​[τj′/αj])\mathrm{toSMT}(\tau_{i}[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}]) is some well formed SMT type. We are almost able to apply ϕ\phi-SMT-Ctor, but we must pick appropriate tj′t_{j}^{\prime}. Whether it’s symbolic or not, let the inner tj′t_{j}^{\prime} there be our tj′t_{j}^{\prime}. By reapplying ϕ\phi-Promote we can find that Γ⊢toSMT⁡(v):v​𝗌𝗆𝗍\Gamma\vdash\mathrm{toSMT}(v):{v}~\mathsf{smt}.

    Immediate: toSMT\mathrm{toSMT} does nothing to the c…𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{\dots}} constructed value nor to the SMT-type τ\tau assigned to it (which is t​𝗌𝗆𝗍{t}~\mathsf{smt} in all cases except for c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}).

∎

Appendix E Type safety

To prove type safety, we prove two properties for every mode of evaluation: first, it is safe, i.e, never yields ⊥\bot; and second, it is type preserving, i.e., well typed inputs yield well typed outputs.

The proofs are fairly conventional. For all but the last step, we prove safety and type preservation simultaneously. We start with expressions and formulas (Lemma E.2), which requires a modest notion of canonical forms (Lemma E.1). Next, we prove that value unification (Lemma E.3) is type preserving, reasoning about unification in general within the lemma showing safety and type preservation for premises (Lemma E.4). After a brief lemma about bindings (Lemma E.5), we can prove that program evaluation is safe (Theorem E.6) and type preserving (Theorem E.7).

Lemma E.1 (Canonical forms for t​𝗌𝗒𝗆{t}~\mathsf{sym}).

If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢v:t​𝗌𝗒𝗆\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash v:{t}~\mathsf{sym} then v=c𝗏𝖺𝗋𝖲𝖬𝖳​[x,t]​()v=c^{\mathsf{SMT}}_{\mathsf{var}}[x,t]().

Proof.

The only typing rule that could have applied is ϕ\phi-SMT-Var. ∎

Lemma E.2 (Term and formula type safety).

If Δ;Φ⊧𝒲\Delta;\Phi\models\mathcal{W} and Δ;Φ⊢F→\Delta;\Phi\vdash\vec{F} and Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta, when either:

  1. (1)

    Δ;Φ;Γ⊢e:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash e:\tau and 𝒲;θ⊢e⇓ev⊥\mathcal{W};\theta\vdash e\Downarrow_{e}v_{\bot}; or

  2. (2)

    Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ϕ:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\phi:\tau and 𝒲;θ⊢ϕ⇓ϕv⊥\mathcal{W};\theta\vdash\phi\Downarrow_{\phi}v_{\bot}

  3. (3)

    Δ;Φ⊢𝖿𝗎𝗇​f​(Xi→:τi→):τ=e\Delta;\Phi\vdash\mathsf{fun}~{f}({\vec{X_{i}}:\vec{\tau_{i}}}):{\tau}={e} and αj→,Xi:τi→⊧θ′\vec{\alpha_{j}},\overrightarrow{X_{i}:\tau_{i}}\models\theta^{\prime} and 𝒲;θ′⊢e⇓ev⊥\mathcal{W};\theta^{\prime}\vdash e\Downarrow_{e}v_{\bot}

then v⊥=vv_{\bot}=v (i.e., v⊥≠⊥v_{\bot}\neq\bot) and Δ;Φ;Γ⊢v:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash v:\tau.

Similarly, when either:

  1. (1)

    if Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ei:τi\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash e_{i}:\tau_{i} and 𝒲;θ⊢ei→⇓evi→\mathcal{W};\theta\vdash\vec{e_{i}}\Downarrow_{e}\vec{v_{i}} then Δ;Φ;Γ⊢vi→⊥:τi→\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\vec{v_{i}}_{\bot}:\vec{\tau_{i}}; and

  2. (2)

    if Δ;Φ;Γ⊢ϕi:τi\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\phi_{i}:\tau_{i} and 𝒲;θ⊢ϕi→⇓ϕ→vi→\mathcal{W};\theta\vdash\vec{\phi_{i}}\Downarrow_{\vec{\phi}}\vec{v_{i}} then Δ;Φ;Γ⊢vi→⊥:τ\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash\vec{v_{i}}_{\bot}:\tau

then vi→⊥=vi→\vec{v_{i}}_{\bot}=\vec{v_{i}} (i.e., it is not ⊥\bot) and Δ;Φ;Γ⊢vi:τi\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash v_{i}:\tau_{i}.

Proof.

By mutual induction on derivations and the length of the vectored expressions/formulas, leaving θ\theta general (for, e.g., ee-Let and ee-Match).

Expressions
  • (ee-Var)

    We have Γ⁡(X)=τ\Gamma(X)=\tau; since Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta, we have θ⁡(X)=v\theta(X)=v (and so ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Var-E didn’t apply). So it must be the case that ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Var applied. We can see further that Δ;Φ;⋅⊢v:τ\Delta;\Phi;\cdot\vdash v:\tau, and we are done by weakening (Lemma D.6).

  • (ee-Const)

    It must be that ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Const applied, and we immediately see that v⊥≠⊥v_{\bot}\neq\bot and kk is well typed in any well formed context by assumption and ee-Const.

  • (ee-Let)

    We know that Γ⊢e1:τ1\Gamma\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{1} and Γ,X:τ1⊢e2:τ2\Gamma,X:\tau_{1}\vdash e_{2}:\tau_{2}. By the IH on e1e_{1}, we know that θ;𝒲⊢e1⇓ev1\theta;\mathcal{W}\vdash e_{1}\Downarrow_{e}v_{1}, so it can’t be the case that ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Let-E applied—it must hae been ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Let. By the IH on e2e_{2}, we know that the final result is also not ⊥\bot and is well typed.

  • (ee-Ctor)

    We have Δ(D)=∀αj→,{…,c:τi→,…}\Delta(D)=\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\{\dots,c:\vec{\tau_{i}},\dots\} and Γ⊢ei:τi​[τj′/αj]\Gamma\vdash e_{i}:\tau_{i}[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}]. By the IH, we know that each of the ei→\vec{e_{i}} must have reduced to non-⊥\bot values, and so ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Ctor-E could not have applied. We can therefore see that each eie_{i} reduces to an appropriately typed viv_{i}, and our resulting value is well typed by ee-Ctor.

  • (ee-Quote)

    Only ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Quote could have applied. By the IH, we know that ϕ\phi reduces to a non-⊥\bot value vv well typed at τ\tau.

  • (ee-Rel)

    We know that p⊆τi→∈Φp\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}\in\Phi and Γ⊢ei:τi\Gamma\vdash e_{i}:\tau_{i}. The IH on ei→\vec{e_{i}} rules out S​t​e​p​s​t​o​EStepstoE-Rel-E1; the typing rule rules out the arity mismatch in ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-E2 and the missing relation in ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-E3. So it must be the case that ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-True or ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Rel-False applied; either way, we yield a 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool}, which is appropriately typed by ee-Const.

  • (ee-Fun)

    We know that f:∀αj→,τi→→τ∈Φf:\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rightarrow\tau\in\Phi and Γ⊢ei:τi​[τj′/αj]\Gamma\vdash e_{i}:\tau_{i}[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}]. The IH on ei→\vec{e_{i}} rules out S​t​e​p​s​t​o​EStepstoE-Fun-E1; the typing rule rules out the arity mismatch in ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun-E2 and the missing function in ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun-E3. So it must be the case that ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Fun applied. Since Δ;Φ⊢F\Delta;\Phi\vdash F, we know by the IH on part (3) that the resulting value is non-⊥\bot and well typed at τ⁡[τj′/αj]\tau[\tau_{j}^{\prime}/\alpha_{j}].

The IH on ei→\vec{e_{i}} rules out S​t​e​p​s​t​o​EStepstoE-Op-E1; the typing rule rules out the arity/domain mismatch in ⇓e\Downarrow_{e}-Op-E2.   • (ee-If)

By the IH on e1e_{1}, we know that e1e_{1} reduces to true\mathrm{true} or false\mathrm{false} (since those are the only values of type 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{bool}).     Therefore either ⇓ϕ\Downarrow_{\phi}-Ctor or ⇓ϕ\Downarrow_{\phi}-Value applied; the resulting value is well typed by the IH or remains well typed, respectively.

By part (1) on αj→,Xi:τi→⊢e:τ\vec{\alpha_{j}},\overrightarrow{X_{i}:\tau_{i}}\vdash e:\tau, using weakening (Lemma D.6) to recover typing in Γ\Gamma.

Vectored expressions and formulas

By induction on the vector length, using parts (1) and (2) in each case. ∎

Lemma E.3 (Value unification preservation).

If Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta when either:

  1. (1)

    Γ⊢X→,τ→⊳Γ′\Gamma\vdash\vec{X},\vec{\tau}\rhd\Gamma^{\prime} and Γ⊢v→:τ→\Gamma\vdash\vec{v}:\vec{\tau} and θ⊢X→∼v→:θ′\theta\vdash\vec{X}\sim\vec{v}:\theta^{\prime}; or

  2. (2)

    Γ⊢X,τ⊳Γ′\Gamma\vdash X,\tau\rhd\Gamma^{\prime} and Γ⊢v:τ\Gamma\vdash v:\tau and θ⊢X∼v⊳θ′\theta\vdash X\sim v\rhd\theta^{\prime};

then Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime}.

Proof.

By induction on the derivation of well typing.

  • (X​τX\tau-Bind)

    Only u​vuv-Bind-Var could have applied, so we have Γ⊢v:τ\Gamma\vdash v:\tau and Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta and must show that Γ,X:τ⊧θ[X↦v]\Gamma,X:\tau\models\theta[X\mapsto v], which we have immediately.

  • (X​τX\tau-Check)

    Here X∈ΓX\in\Gamma, so it must be that θ⁡(X)\theta(X) is defined. One of three rules could have applied:

    • (u​vuv-Eq-Var)

      We have Γ′=Γ\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma and θ′=θ\theta^{\prime}=\theta, so Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime} by assumption.

    • (u​vuv-Ctor)

      By the IH, we know that Γ′​m​o​d​e​l​s​θ′\Gamma^{\prime}models\theta^{\prime}.

    • (u​vuv-Constant)

      As for u​vuv-Eq-Var, we have Γ′=Γ\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma and θ′=θ\theta^{\prime}=\theta, so Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime} by assumption.

  • (X​τX\tau-All)

    It must be that u→​v→\vec{u}\vec{v}-All applied; by the IH on each sub-derivation, we can find that Γi⊧θi\Gamma_{i}\models\theta_{i}, and so Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime} in particular.

∎

User code will never directly trigger a use of u​vuv-Eq-Var directly, because the unification rules won’t call value unification with a defined LHS (we’d just use u​uuu-BB instead). But a use of u→​v→\vec{u}\vec{v}-All could lead to a variable being unified early on and then used again in the same unification process.

Lemma E.4 (Premise preservation and safety).

If Δ;Φ;Γ⊢P⊳Γ′\Delta;\Phi;\Gamma\vdash P\rhd\Gamma^{\prime} and Δ;Φ⊧F→\Delta;\Phi\models\vec{F} and Δ;Φ⊧𝒲\Delta;\Phi\models\mathcal{W} and Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta then if F→;𝒲;θ⊢P→θ⊥′\vec{F};\mathcal{W};\theta\vdash P\rightarrow\theta^{\prime}_{\bot} then:

  1. (1)

    θ⊥′=θ′\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}=\theta^{\prime} (i.e., it is not ⊥\bot); and

  2. (2)

    Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime}.

Proof.

By induction on the premise typing derivation, followed by cases on the step taken.

  • (PP-PosAtom)

    We have:

    p⊆τi→∈ΦΓ⊢Xi→,τi→⊳Γ′p\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}\in\Phi\quad\quad\Gamma\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rhd\Gamma^{\prime}

    The only rule that could have applied is PosAtom, i.e., v→∈𝒲⁡(p)\vec{v}\in\mathcal{W}(p) and θ⊢Xi→∼vi→:θ⊥′\theta\vdash\vec{X_{i}}\sim\vec{v_{i}}:\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}. We must show that θ⊥′=θ′\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}=\theta^{\prime} and Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime}.

    Since Δ;Φ⊧𝒲\Delta;\Phi\models\mathcal{W}, we know that ⋅⊢vi→:τi→\cdot\vdash\vec{v_{i}}:\vec{\tau_{i}}; by weakening we have Γ⊢vi→:τi→\Gamma\vdash\vec{v_{i}}:\vec{\tau_{i}} (Lemma D.6).

    Syntactically, we know that Xi→\vec{X_{i}} are all variables and that vi→\vec{v_{i}} are all values. For each one, therefore only two unification rules could possibly apply: u​uuu-BB (XiX_{i} is bound) and u​uuu-FB (XiX_{i} is free). In particular, u​uuu-FF cannot apply, and so we cannot produce ⊥\bot, so θ⊥′=θ′=θ​θi→\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}=\theta^{\prime}=\theta\vec{\theta_{i}}. By Lemma E.3, we know that Γ′⊧θ​θi\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta\theta_{i} for each ii, and so Γ′⊧θ​θi→\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta\vec{\theta_{i}}.

  • (PP-NegAtom)

    We have:

    p⊆τi→∈ΦΓ⊢Xi→,τi→⊳Γ\begin{array}[]{c}p\subseteq\vec{\tau_{i}}\in\Phi\quad\quad\Gamma\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau_{i}}\rhd\Gamma\end{array}

    Two rules are possible: NegAtom and NegAtom-E. We must show that the latter cannot apply and that the former preserves typing.

    Since Γ⊧θ\Gamma\models\theta, it must be that case that each Xi→∈dom⁡(θ)\vec{X_{i}}\in\mathrm{dom}(\theta), and so NegAtom-E cannot have applied. It remains to be seen that Γ⊧θ′\Gamma\models\theta^{\prime}—but in NegAtom we have θ=θ′\theta=\theta^{\prime}, and so we are done.

  • (PP-EqCtor-BF)

    We have:

    Δ(D)=∀αj→,{…,c:τi→,…}Γ⊢Y,τ⁡[τj′→/αj→]⊳ΓXi→⊈ΓΓ⊢Xi→,τi→​[τj′→/αj→]⊳Γ′\begin{array}[]{c}\Delta(D)=\forall\vec{\alpha_{j}},\{\dots,c:\vec{\tau_{i}},\dots\}\\ \Gamma\vdash Y,\tau[\vec{\tau_{j}^{\prime}}/\vec{\alpha_{j}}]\rhd\Gamma\quad\quad\vec{X_{i}}\nsubseteq\Gamma\quad\quad\Gamma\vdash\vec{X_{i}},\vec{\tau_{i}}[\vec{\tau_{j}^{\prime}}/\vec{\alpha_{j}}]\rhd\Gamma^{\prime}\end{array}

    The only rule that could have applied is EqCtor, where θ⊢Y​c​(Xi→):θ⊥′\theta\vdash Y~c(\vec{X_{i}}):\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}. We must show that θ⊥′=θ′\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}=\theta^{\prime} (i.e., it is not ⊥\bot) and that Γ′⊧θ′\Gamma^{\prime}\models\theta^{\prime}.

    Since Γ⊢Y,τ⁡[τj′→/αj→]⊳Γ\Gamma\vdash Y,\tau[\vec{\tau_{j}^{\prime}}/\vec{\alpha_{j}}]\rhd\Gamma, it must be the case that Y∈dom⁡(Γ)Y\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma) and so θ⁡(Y)=v\theta(Y)=v (and so ⋅⊢v:τ⁡[τj′→/αj→]\cdot\vdash v:\tau[\vec{\tau_{j}^{\prime}}/\vec{\alpha_{j}}], which also holds under Γ\Gamma thanks to weakening (Lemma D.6)).

    Only two rules could have applied to show θ⊢Y​c​(Xi→):θ⊥′\theta\vdash Y~c(\vec{X_{i}}):\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}: u​uuu-BF (when some of Xi→\vec{X_{i}} are unbound) or u​uuu-BB (when all of the Xi→\vec{X_{i}} are bound). In either case, u​uuu-FF can’t have a applied, and so θ⊥′=θ′\theta^{\prime}_{\bot}=\theta^{\prime}.

    One of two rules could have applied: u​vuv-Eq-Var or u​vuv-Ctor.

Appendix F Model-theoretic semantics

We have focused on the operational semantics of Formulog, as it helps us to reason about type safety. However, since we have kept Formulog close to Datalog, it is also possible to give a model-theoretic semantics to a Formulog program. First, all ML functions and expressions are desugared into Datalog rules; this translation is relatively straightforward, with the trickiest part being the translation of non-mutually exclusive patterns occurring in match expressions. For each primitive operator, we introduce a (possibly infinite) EDB relation that defines that operator; for example, the addition operator  + is represented through a ternary relation add(xx, yy, zz), which states that zz is the sum of xx and yy. Terms of the form p⁡(w∗)p(w^{*}) (i.e., invocations of predicates as functions) are translated to aggregate predicates. Formulog requires the use of these terms, as well as negation, to be stratified; thus, the program resulting from the translation can be given a perfect model semantics in line with stratified negation (Apt et al., 1988; Przymusinski, 1988; Van Gelder, 1989) and stratified aggregation (Mumick et al., 1990).

For a small example, consider this Formulog program:

⬇
fun length(Xs: ’a list) : bv[32] =
match Xs with
| [] => 0
| _ :: T => 1 + length(T)
end
ok :- length([1, 2, 3]) = 3.

This would be translated into a program like this:

⬇
length([], 0).
length(_ :: T, Z) :-
length(T, L),
add(1, L, Z).
ok :- length([1, 2, 3], 3).

Note that the rules defining the length predicate violate the range restriction, and in fact define an infinite relation. This does not pose a fundamental problem to the model theory. To make this program evaluable, we could rewrite the length predicate’s definition (and its uses) via the magic set transformation; the resulting relations would meet the range restriction. While the magic set transformation can turn a stratified program into a non-stratified program, there are techniques to either restore stratification (Meskes and Noack, 1993) or correctly evaluate the non-stratified program (Mumick et al., 1990; Balbin et al., 1991).
